forces.title: SHANTI Act opens civil nuclear sector to private and foreign participation
forces.description: The landmark SHANTI Act in December 2025 replaced legacy nuclear regimes, opening India's civil nuclear ecosystem to private and foreign participation. This structural shift allows private entities to build, own, operate, and decommission nuclear plants, while retaining state control over fuel-cycle activities and strengthening the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB). It creates a new framework for global players to engage in India’s nuclear build-out through India-incorporated joint ventures.
forces.source_title: How India’s nuclear ambition can power the next global clean energy push

forces.title: India's 100 GW nuclear target by 2047 signals massive capacity expansion
forces.description: The Nuclear Energy Mission sets an ambitious target for India to reach 100 GW of nuclear power capacity by 2047, a tenfold scale-up from the current 8.9 GW. This commitment positions nuclear energy as a mainstream clean baseload energy pillar, targeting a multi-technology setup including PHWRs, large reactors, SMRs, and advanced technologies. This long-term ambition drives significant investment and development opportunities in the sector.
forces.source_title: How India’s nuclear ambition can power the next global clean energy push

forces.title: INR20,000 crore budgetary push accelerates advanced reactor R&D and localization
forces.description: The National Nuclear Energy Mission, backed by a significant INR20,000 crore commitment, accelerates research and innovation in Small Modular Reactors (SMRs), Bharat Small Reactors (BSRs), and advanced reactor R&D. This push also focuses on localizing India’s nuclear supply chain. This financial and institutional foundation aims to position India at the forefront of next-generation nuclear development, creating opportunities for technology partnerships and co-development.
forces.source_title: How India’s nuclear ambition can power the next global clean energy push

forces.title: Private operator entry opens new models for nuclear asset ownership
forces.description: Enabling private players to become nuclear asset owners or operators shifts India's nuclear market from a transaction-led vendor market to a long-term ecosystem play. This opens new business models around captive power, industrial decarbonization, operations and maintenance (O&M), and lifecycle services. For global players, this allows deeper participation through collaborations and leveraging India’s nascent nuclear ecosystem with bankable commercial use cases, marking a significant market liberalization.
forces.source_title: How India’s nuclear ambition can power the next global clean energy push

forces.title: FDI restrictions and regulatory uncertainty hinder direct foreign participation
forces.description: Atomic energy remains a prohibited sector under India’s Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) policy, restricting foreign participation in licensed nuclear activities. While there are indications the government may permit up to 49% foreign investment, amendments are yet to be notified. This regulatory uncertainty means foreign players are required to participate through Indian-incorporated vehicles or structured partnerships, limiting direct ownership and necessitating close monitoring for clarity on participation contours.
forces.source_title: How India’s nuclear ambition can power the next global clean energy push

forces.title: Bharat Small Reactors offer low CAPEX and stable O&M, de-risking investments
forces.description: Bharat Small Reactors (BSRs), India’s indigenous SMRs, boast estimated CAPEX of INR15 Cr/MW (US$1.6M/MW), making them significantly more cost-effective than many global designs. Coupled with stable O&M costs and sovereign fuel-cycle control, BSRs offer predictable, long-term cash flows over their 40-year life. This attractive cost structure materially de-risks nuclear investments, positioning BSRs as an infrastructure-grade opportunity to expand nuclear capacity.
forces.source_title: How India’s nuclear ambition can power the next global clean energy push

forces.title: SMRs provide baseload power, complementing intermittent renewables for net-zero
forces.description: Small Modular Reactors (SMRs) are gaining traction as a promising low-carbon baseload alternative to coal, without compromising reliability, security, or grid stability. SMRs can be co-located with retiring coal plants, easing transition logistics, and offer flexible, grid-responsive operation alongside renewables. This complementarity makes SMRs crucial for India's energy transition, helping to balance emission reduction goals with energy security and affordability.
forces.source_title: Eigenvectors of net zero: Building a resilient energy future

forces.title: India's abundant thorium reserves offer long-term energy security
forces.description: India possesses one of the world’s largest thorium reserves (approx. 1.07 million tonnes), primarily in coastal monazite sands. This vast resource underpins India's Three-Stage Nuclear Power Programme, focused on sustainable energy production and reducing reliance on limited uranium. Significant progress in thorium fuel cycle development and the design of Advanced Heavy Water Reactors (AHWRs) leverage this domestic advantage for future energy security and low-waste production.
forces.source_title: Eigenvectors of net zero: Building a resilient energy future

forces.title: Increased government capital expenditure directly funds nuclear project expansion
forces.description: Increased government capital expenditure directly supports infrastructure development, including funding for new nuclear power projects and capacity expansion. This accelerates growth in the nuclear sector, aligning with India's ambitious targets and strategic plans. Public funding is critical for the capital-intensive nature of nuclear energy, enabling faster deployment and greater self-reliance.
forces.source_title: Eigenvectors of net zero: Building a resilient energy future

forces.title: Rising fiscal deficit threatens government support and increases borrowing costs
forces.description: A higher fiscal deficit signals greater government financial strain, potentially leading to reduced budgetary allocations for nuclear subsidies, slower payments, or a less supportive policy environment. It can also lead to higher government borrowing, potentially crowding out private investment and increasing interest rates, thereby raising financing costs for capital-intensive nuclear energy investments. This directly impacts the pace and scale of nuclear build-out.
forces.source_title: Eigenvectors of net zero: Building a resilient energy future

forces.title: AI-driven innovation and private investment accelerate SMR development
forces.description: Artificial Intelligence's substantial energy demand is accelerating the innovation timeline for clean energy solutions, particularly Small Modular Reactors (SMRs). Private investment, especially from hyperscalers like Microsoft, is driving direct investment into nuclear microgeneration. This shift positions tech firms as developers of power, drawing capital and accelerating innovation in the SMR space, creating a virtuous loop between AI demand and clean energy capacity expansion.
forces.source_title: AI's dual promise: Enabling positive climate outcomes and powering the energy transition

viewpoints.title: Nuclear energy crucial for India's energy security amidst geopolitical volatility
viewpoints.description: CareEdge emphasizes nuclear energy's strategic role in reducing India's reliance on imported oil and gas, particularly in the face of 'stop-start' US-Iran conflict and Strait of Hormuz disruptions. By diversifying its energy mix with nuclear power, India can insulate itself from persistent external shocks and enhance macroeconomic stability, following models like France which is oil/gas deficient. This shift is critical for long-term energy resilience.

viewpoints.title: India's nuclear ambition shifts to strategic pillar for dependable, low-carbon power
viewpoints.description: EY-Parthenon highlights India's decisive shift towards nuclear energy as a strategic pillar, aiming for 100 GW by 2047. This is driven by the need for dependable, round-the-clock, low-carbon power to balance rising demand with energy security and decarbonization. Policy reforms, regulatory strengthening, budgetary commitments, and opening to private/international participation create significant opportunities for global engagement across the nuclear value chain.
viewpoints.source_title: How India’s nuclear ambition can power the next global clean energy push

viewpoints.title: Indian civil nuclear market now a procurement reality, open for global players
viewpoints.description: The Nuclear Business Platform asserts that India's nuclear ambition is no longer aspirational but a procurement reality, especially after the SHANTI Act opened the civil nuclear market to private and foreign participation. With a 100 GW target by 2047 and a market valued at US$214 billion, it presents a significant, narrow window of opportunity for international reactor vendors, engineering firms, equipment manufacturers, and financiers to build relationships and define their roles.
viewpoints.source_title: How India’s nuclear ambition can power the next global clean energy push

viewpoints.title: Nuclear energy remains a long-term priority with evolutionary, not transformative, trajectory
viewpoints.description: Raju Kumar from EY views nuclear energy as a long-term strategic priority within India's clean energy transition. While recent policy changes, like allowing private sector participation, signal commitment, nuclear energy remains capital-intensive and long-gestation. He expects Budget 2026 to reinforce its long-term role, with near-term capacity additions driven by other clean energy technologies. SMRs are noted as an early-stage technology, suggesting a cautious approach to immediate large-scale deployment.
viewpoints.source_title: Budget 2026 expectations: India’s energy future and clean energy transition

viewpoints.title: Nuclear energy moves from promise to value, crucial for India's net-zero transition
viewpoints.description: CII highlights that civil nuclear energy is gaining traction and moving from promises to a real value proposition through the Nuclear Energy Mission, targeting 100 GW by 2047. It emphasizes SMRs' potential for baseload complementarity to renewables, leveraging thorium reserves, and de-risking investments through legislative reforms. Nuclear energy is seen as balancing emission reduction goals with security, reliability, and affordability, essential for India's net-zero energy future.
viewpoints.source_title: Eigenvectors of net zero: Building a resilient energy future

viewpoints.title: AI's energy demand accelerating SMR innovation and private investment
viewpoints.description: KPMG observes that Artificial Intelligence's growing energy appetite is accelerating the innovation timeline for clean technologies, including Small Modular Reactors (SMRs). Hyperscalers like Microsoft are directly investing in nuclear microgeneration, shifting tech firms from mere power consumers to energy developers. This private capital infusion, driven by guaranteed demand, is compressing development times for SMRs, indicating a self-reinforcing loop where AI demand drives clean energy innovation.
viewpoints.source_title: AI's dual promise: Enabling positive climate outcomes and powering the energy transition

National budgetary push accelerates R&D and localization efforts, creating opportunities for technology partnerships and co-development.
